title: No Instagram account? You can still see what local shops post in their stories | Sponsored | rutlandherald.com
text:
A lot of small-town news never makes the paper. The bakery sold out of maple scones by ten. The diner closed early because the plow had not come through yet. The farm stand finally has sweet corn. More and more, updates like these go out as Instagram stories, and a day later they are gone.
That is a problem if you are not on Instagram.
Plenty of Vermonters are not. Plenty more signed up once, forgot the password and never went back. Meanwhile the ski shop posts the morning's snow report as a story, the rec department announces cancellations the same way, and the Friday specials at half the restaurants in the county live there and nowhere else.
You do not need an account to read public stories. Several free websites will show them in an ordinary browser, on any phone or computer. I tried five approaches over two weeks this fall, on a phone and on an aging desktop, and graded them the way a teacher would.
Three things to know first
It only works for public accounts. That covers most businesses, town offices, school athletic pages and event organizers, because they want to be seen. Private accounts, which is what most individuals use, cannot be viewed this way. Any site that says otherwise should be closed on the spot.
You will not show up in the viewer list. The shop will never know you looked.
You never need to hand over a password. More on that further down.
The report card
StoriesIG: A
This is the one I would set up on a parent's or grandparent's phone. There is a single box. Type the business's Instagram name, press the button, and today's stories appear, followed by the older highlights the account has saved. It worked on the first try nearly every time. My only two misses came on an afternoon when Instagram was down for everybody.
It can also save a story to your phone as a picture or a short video, which turned out to be more useful than I expected. When a hardware store posted its holiday hours as a story, I saved the slide and had it handy all week. If you want aninsta story viewer that works without an account or an app, start here.
The site does show ads. They are the ordinary kind and they stay out of the way.
AnonyIG: A minus
Very nearly as good. It is easier to browse when an account keeps a long shelf of highlights, like an outfitter with a folder for every season. Twice the search hung long enough that I gave up and reloaded, and that is the only reason it missed first place.
InstaNavigation: B
This one does one thing especially well. It shows exactly when each story went up. When you are trying to work out whether a road closure notice is from this morning or yesterday, that detail matters. It slowed down with accounts that post many videos back to back.
iGram: B minus
iGram is built for saving rather than browsing. Instead of typing an account name, you paste the link to a specific story or video, and it hands you the file. Great if a friend has texted you a link. Clumsy if you just want to see what the co-op posted this morning.
Asking someone to show you on their phone: incomplete
It works, and for years it was how most of us did it. It is not private, though. Their name lands in the viewer list, and you have to wait until someone is around who is logged in.
At a glance
Option | Grade | Needs an account | Browse by name | Best for |
StoriesIG | A | No | Yes | Everyday checking and saving |
AnonyIG | A minus | No | Yes | Long highlight collections |
InstaNavigation | B | No | Yes | Knowing when a story was posted |
iGram | B minus | No | No, needs a link | Saving a video someone sent you |
Someone else's phone | Incomplete | Yes | Yes | When nothing else is handy |
Making it a one-tap habit
What made this stick for me was the home screen. On an iPhone, open the viewer site in Safari, tap the share button and choose Add to Home Screen. On an Android phone, open it in Chrome, tap the three dots and pick the same option. Now it sits next to the weather app and opens like one.
From there it takes about ten seconds. Tap, type the account name, read. I keep the handful I check on a sticky note by the coffee maker: the bakery, the ski shop, the library, the farmers market. Most mornings that is all the local news I need.
Habits worth keeping
Never type your Instagram password into one of these sites. A viewer for public stories has no reason to know who you are, and a site that asks is collecting accounts. Those tend to end up for sale as fake followers.
Skip anything that insists you install an app or a browser add-on. The websites above do the whole job without one.
And be a good neighbor about what you save. A screenshot of the pizza place's specials is for your own fridge door. Reposting a local photographer's foliage shots without asking is something else, and for some of them those photos are how they pay the bills.
The bottom line
To see what a café, a farm or the town office posted today, all you need is a browser and one dependable viewer site. Over my two weeks, StoriesIG was the most reliable of the group, with AnonyIG close behind. Keep one of the others bookmarked as a backup for the rare day the first choice has trouble.
summary: Meanwhile the ski shop posts the morning's snow report as a story, the rec department announces cancellations the same way, and the Friday specials at half the restaurants in the county live there and nowhere else. Type the business's Instagram name, press the button, and today's stories appear, followed by the older highlights the account has saved.
